<reason>A built a coherent, consistently defended sufficiency thesis (consent = information + competence + voluntariness, with externalities treated as separate wrongs) and used it to systematically show that B's early examples (miners, payday loans, kidney sales) smuggled in deception, desperation, or third-party harm rather than showing pure consent failing on its own. B's strongest counter-move — the "definitional trap" charge plus the tailored gambler/derivatives example — was clever and forced real engagement, but A's Pressure Questions and Rebuttal 2 exposed that B's key distinction ("delivering wanted value" vs "extracting value via manufactured error") collapses once the buyer is conceded to be fully informed and simply human-and-hopeful, and that "fraud without words" concedes there was no actual fraud. B's closing retreated to restating the definitional-trap framing rather than defending the gambler distinction against that direct hit, leaving A's last word unanswered on the decisive example. B's third-party "structural dependency" point on pollution was a genuinely strong, under-exploited angle, but it wasn't pressed hard enough in the closing to offset the loss on the gambler exchange. A's repeated clipping (losing its final synthesis line in three separate speeches) is a real execution cost that trims the margin, but doesn't overturn the substantive edge A built through the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 response to the gambler case (A4.1–A4.2): pointing out the gambler "wanted" the derivative and that "fraud without words" concedes no actual misrepresentation occurred, which B's closing never directly answered.</best_rebuttal>
